title: How Nature Works in Harmony
subject: Science
description: Habitats and their biotic and abiotic components, populations, communities and ecosystems, producers, consumers and decomposers, food chains, trophic levels and food webs, species relationships, cascading changes, ecosystem benefits and threats, protected areas and sustainable farming.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is a habitat?
options: The place where an organism lives
The group of organisms of one kind
The food an organism depends upon
The climate zone of a whole region
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a habitat simply as the place where an organism lives — it can even be as small as the bark of a tree. A group of one kind of organism is a population, not a habitat.

questions.question: Which example does the chapter give to show that a habitat can be very small?
questions.explanation: The text says a habitat 'could even be just the bark of a tree'. The other places are habitats too, but the bark is the specific tiny example the chapter uses.

questions.question: The living beings recorded in a habitat (fish, grass, trees, birds) are termed its —
questions.explanation: Living beings are the biotic components; non-living things such as water and soil are the abiotic components. 'Physical conditions' refers to abiotic factors like air, sunlight and temperature.

questions.question: From Table 12.1, which pair lists one biotic and one abiotic component of the pond habitat?
questions.explanation: In the pond column, fish is a living being (biotic) and water is a non-living thing (abiotic). Grass/trees and birds/fish are both-biotic pairs; soil/water are both abiotic.

questions.question: In a pond, from where do fish obtain their abiotic need of oxygen?
questions.explanation: The chapter says fish obtain biotic needs such as food from small plants and animals, and abiotic needs such as oxygen from water.

questions.question: According to the chapter, from which sources does a pond fish obtain its BIOTIC needs?
questions.explanation: Biotic needs are those met by other living things — food from small plants and animals. Oxygen from water is an abiotic need; space and shelter are conditions the pond provides, not biotic sources.

questions.question: A snake that comes out at night and a rodent active by day live in the same forest. What does this show?
options: Night animals need a cooler habitat than day animals do
Organisms coexist by using one habitat under different conditions
Organisms in one habitat always face identical conditions
Snakes and rodents cannot share a single habitat for long
questions.explanation: The forest is warm by day and cool by night, so the two animals face different conditions in the same place. The chapter calls this coexisting in harmony — not identical conditions.

questions.question: Different habitats offer different living conditions, and every organism needs specific conditions to survive.
questions.explanation: This is the conclusion drawn from Activity 12.1: pond and forest provide different conditions, which is why some organisms live on land and others in water.

questions.question: In the chapter's forest example, the habitat is cool during the day and warm at night.
questions.explanation: It is the reverse: the forest 'might be warm during the day and cool at night'. The snake (night) and rodent (day) therefore meet different temperatures.

questions.question: Which pair names two plants that the chapter lists as living in a pond?
questions.explanation: The pond plants named are algae, diatoms, duckweeds and lotus. Snails, ducks and dragonflies are animals, so the other pairs mix a plant with an animal.

questions.question: Which statement about the two habitats compared in Activity 12.1 is NOT correct?
options: The non-living things are the same in both habitats
Both habitats contain living beings as well as non-living things
The types of living beings differ between the two habitats
A pond and a forest each provide conditions suited to their organisms
questions.explanation: The chapter says both habitats have living and non-living things, but 'the types of living beings are different and the non-living things also vary'. So the non-living things are not the same.

questions.question: A group of fish of the same kind living together in a pond is called a —
questions.explanation: A population is a group of the same type of organism in a habitat at a given time. A community has many different populations; an ecosystem also includes abiotic components.

questions.question: What does a community comprise?
options: All abiotic conditions present in a habitat
Organisms of one kind counted at one time
Different populations sharing the same habitat
Individuals of one species sharing a habitat
questions.explanation: A community is made of different populations (plants, animals, microorganisms) in the same habitat. One species' individuals form a population; abiotic conditions are not part of a community.

questions.question: In Activity 12.2, students counted 20 plants of one kind in a 1 m × 1 m plot. What does the number 20 represent?
options: The community of that plant in the plot
The ecosystem of that plant in the plot
The trophic level of that plant in the plot
The population of that plant in the plot
questions.explanation: Counting individuals of one type at a given place and time gives its population. A community would need different kinds of organisms; a trophic level is a feeding position.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT part of the chapter's definition of a population?
options: The organisms must feed at the same trophic level
The organisms must all be of the same kind
The organisms must live in the same habitat
The organisms are considered at a given time
questions.explanation: A population is 'a group of the same type of organisms in a habitat at a given time'. Trophic level is a food-chain idea and is not part of the definition.

questions.question: If a habitat had only one type of living organism, what does the chapter say could happen?
options: A new community, since the organisms would soon become different
Competition and scarcity, since all need the same food, water and space
Rapid growth and plenty, since no other species competes for food
A stable balance, since one species cannot cause an imbalance
questions.explanation: Identical organisms have identical requirements, so they compete for the same food, water and space — leading to possible scarcity, not plenty or stability.

questions.question: A community is made up of different populations that share the same habitat.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a community comprises different populations sharing the same habitat, which interact and depend on one another.

questions.question: The plants, animals and microorganisms of a habitat together form its population.
questions.explanation: Together they form the community. A population is only one type of organism; the biotic components as a whole make up the community.

questions.question: Which of these belong to the COMMUNITY of a habitat?
questions.explanation: The community is formed by the biotic components — plants, animals and microorganisms. Sunlight and temperature are abiotic components and belong to the ecosystem, not the community.

questions.question: Refer to Fig. 12.19 (population inside community inside ecosystem). Which statement is WRONG?
options: A community is larger than a population
A community is smaller than an ecosystem
A population is part of a community
An ecosystem is part of a community
questions.explanation: The nesting is population → community → ecosystem. A community is part of an ecosystem, not the other way round, so statement (iii) in the exercise is the wrong one.

questions.question: Fig. 12.7 shows levels of organisation from smallest to largest. Which order is correct?
questions.explanation: One organism is an individual; many of the same kind form a population; different populations form a community; the community plus abiotic components forms an ecosystem.

questions.question: A pond holds a population of fish, a population of frogs and a population of snails. Together these populations are called —
questions.explanation: Several different populations sharing one habitat make up a community. 'Population' applies to only one kind of organism at a time.

questions.question: Which part of a flower is the male reproductive part?
questions.explanation: Stamens are the male parts that burst to release pollen; carpels are the female parts. Sepals are green leafy structures and petals are the coloured parts.

questions.question: What does the chapter call pollination?
options: Carrying pollen from stamens to carpels of the same or different flowers
Bursting of stamens to release yellow pollen grains into the wind
Formation of fruits and seeds inside the carpel after flowering
Movement of nectar from the petals to visiting insects and birds
questions.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from stamens to carpels (of the same and/or different flowers). Fruit and seed formation follows pollination but is not pollination itself.

questions.question: Which of these are named in the chapter as carriers of pollen?
questions.explanation: Wind, water, insects, bats and birds help carry pollen. Earthworms live in soil and fungi are decomposers — neither is listed as a pollinator.

questions.question: Pollination is described as essential for —
questions.explanation: The chapter states that pollination 'is essential for the formation of fruits and seeds'.

questions.question: In Activity 12.3, Pond A (with fish) had fewer dragonflies than Pond B. Why?
options: Fish compete with dragonflies for pollen
Fish drive bees and butterflies away
Fish eat dragonfly larvae in the pond
Fish eat the adult dragonflies above the water
questions.explanation: Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so fewer larvae grow into adults and the pond with fish has fewer dragonflies.

questions.question: With fewer dragonflies around a pond, what did the study find?
options: Fewer bees, flies and butterflies survive
More dragonfly larvae in the water
Fewer flowering plants near the pond
More bees, flies and butterflies survive
questions.explanation: Dragonflies eat flies, bees and butterflies; with fewer dragonflies, more of these insects were found near the pond.

questions.question: Why may flowers near a pond WITH fish produce more seeds than flowers near a pond without fish?
options: More pollinators survive because fish reduce the dragonflies that eat them
Fish fertilise the nearby soil, so plants make more flowers and seeds
Dragonflies pollinate flowers, and fish help dragonflies breed
Fish eat the bees and butterflies that would damage the flowers
questions.explanation: Fish → fewer dragonfly larvae → fewer dragonflies → more bees, flies and butterflies → more pollination → more seeds. Dragonflies are predators of pollinators, not pollinators themselves.

questions.question: In Fig. 12.4, red arrows are direct effects and green arrows indirect. The effect of fish on the St. John's wort plant is —
questions.explanation: Fish do not touch the plant; they act through dragonflies and pollinators. Since more seeds are produced near fish ponds, the overall effect on the plant is indirect and positive.

questions.question: Which of these is a DIRECT effect in the pond study?
questions.explanation: Fish directly eat larvae. The rise in pollinators, flowers and seeds happens through a chain of other organisms, so those are indirect effects.

questions.question: In the pond study, the pond with fish had more dragonflies than the pond without fish.
questions.explanation: Pond A with fish had FEWER dragonflies, because fish eat dragonfly larvae.

questions.question: Dragonflies usually eat flies, bees and butterflies.
questions.explanation: The chapter says dragonflies usually eat flies, bees and butterflies — that is why fewer dragonflies means more of these pollinators.

questions.question: Suppose humans overfish Pond A and remove most of its fish. Predict the chain of changes.
options: Dragonflies fall, pollinators rise, nearby seed production rises
Dragonflies rise, pollinators rise, nearby seed production rises
Dragonflies fall, pollinators fall, nearby seed production drops
Dragonflies rise, pollinators fall, nearby seed production drops
questions.explanation: Removing fish lets more dragonfly larvae survive, so dragonflies increase, eat more bees and butterflies, and fewer flowers get pollinated — seed production falls.

questions.question: 'A frog eats insects.' Under which criterion of Activity 12.4 does this interaction fall?
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Both frog and insects are living, so this is an interaction among biotic components (Criterion 3).

questions.question: 'Earthworms live in moist soil.' This is an interaction —
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Earthworms (biotic) depend on moist soil (abiotic), so it is a biotic–abiotic interaction (Criterion 1).

questions.question: 'Frogs and fish may compete for small insect larvae.' Which type of interaction is this?
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Frogs, fish and larvae are all living things, so competition for food is an interaction among biotic components.

questions.question: 'A fish lays eggs in water.' Table 12.3 places this under which criterion?
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: The fish (biotic) uses water (abiotic) for reproduction, which Criterion 1 describes as abiotic components influencing life processes like reproduction.

questions.question: 'A fish lays eggs in water near vegetation to protect them from other fish or frogs.' Table 12.3 classifies this as an interaction —
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Although water is involved, the reason for the behaviour is protection from other fish and frogs — living things. The table therefore lists it under interactions among biotic components.

questions.question: 'Air current is blowing slowly on the water surface creating gentle waves.' This is an interaction —
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Air and water are both abiotic, so this is an interaction between two abiotic components that changes a physical feature of the habitat.

questions.question: 'The soil near the pond is moist.' Which criterion fits this observation?
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Moist soil results from soil (abiotic) interacting with water (abiotic). Table 12.3 lists it under Criterion 2.

questions.question: Which type of interaction may influence the PHYSICAL characteristics of a habitat?
options: Between a population and its community
questions.explanation: Criterion 2 says interactions between two abiotic components (e.g. sunlight heating the day) may influence the physical characteristics of a habitat.

questions.question: Which of these examples does Table 12.3 list under Criterion 1 (biotic–abiotic interactions)?
options: Many microbes are present in the pond
A fish lays eggs in water
The soil near the pond is moist
questions.explanation: Microbes in pond water and fish laying eggs in water involve a living thing and water. The snake eating fish is biotic–biotic; moist soil near the pond is abiotic–abiotic.

questions.question: In Table 12.3, 'a water snake eats fish' is an example of an interaction between biotic and abiotic components.
questions.explanation: Both snake and fish are living organisms, so this is an interaction among biotic components (Criterion 3).

questions.question: Which abiotic inputs does the chapter say plants need to produce food?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are essential for producing food in plants. Oxygen is used for respiration, not food making.

questions.question: Which of these show BIOTIC components influencing ABIOTIC components?
options: Roots hold soil in place and prevent erosion
Soil supplies essential nutrients to plants
Water provides fish with dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: Plants changing the air (oxygen) and roots protecting soil are living things affecting non-living ones. Soil feeding plants and water supplying oxygen are abiotic components helping biotic ones.

questions.question: Which statement about biotic and abiotic components is NOT correct?
options: Abiotic components are never changed by living things
Water is essential for every living organism in an ecosystem
Plants retain soil moisture and help cool the atmosphere
Many nutrients in soil come from the decomposition process
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that abiotic components are also influenced by biotic ones — plants release oxygen, roots prevent erosion and plants cool the atmosphere.

questions.question: If all plants were removed from a hill slope, which change does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: Air would get cooler as fewer plants release heat
Soil would erode more easily as roots no longer hold it
Soil would become richer as fewer roots take nutrients
Soil would stay moister as no leaves shade it
questions.explanation: Roots hold soil in place and prevent erosion, and plants retain soil moisture and cool the atmosphere. Removing them makes erosion likely and the soil drier.

questions.question: Air provides carbon dioxide for respiration in plants and animals.
questions.explanation: Air provides OXYGEN for respiration. Carbon dioxide is used by plants, along with sunlight and water, to make food.

questions.question: Which option correctly pairs a need with the abiotic component that supplies it?
questions.explanation: Air gives oxygen for respiration; soil provides the medium and nutrients; sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are needed for making food.

questions.question: Biotic and abiotic components of a habitat interacting with each other form —
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is formed by the interaction of biotic components (plants, animals, microbes) with abiotic components (air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature).

questions.question: In Fig. 12.6, which ecosystem is described as human-made?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that farmland is a human-made ecosystem, while mountains, forests and grassland are natural terrestrial ecosystems.

questions.question: Which statement about ecosystems is NOT correct?
options: Ponds, rivers and lakes are aquatic ecosystems
Different ecosystems may overlap and interact
Ecosystems are always large areas like forests and rivers
A large banyan tree can be treated as an ecosystem
questions.explanation: The chapter says ecosystems 'can be large or small' — even a single large tree like a banyan, mango or pilkhan counts as one.

questions.question: Which of these are TERRESTRIAL ecosystems according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Terrestrial (land) ecosystems include forests, farms and large trees. Ponds and lakes are aquatic ecosystems.

questions.question: Fig. 12.6 shows a small river among mountains, forests, grassland and farmland. What does the figure illustrate?
options: A food web linking river and farmland
A community of populations in a river
Overlap of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems
questions.explanation: The river is aquatic while the mountains, forests, grassland and farmland are terrestrial. The figure shows these ecosystems overlapping and interacting.

questions.question: Ecosystems can be large or small.
questions.explanation: A forest is a large ecosystem while a single pilkhan or banyan tree can be a small one, so ecosystems vary in size.

questions.question: A single pilkhan tree is too small to be considered an ecosystem.
questions.explanation: The chapter names 'large trees like banyan, mango, or pilkhan' as examples of terrestrial ecosystems — size does not disqualify them.

questions.question: Organisms in an ecosystem interact with abiotic components for —
questions.explanation: The chapter states that organisms interact with abiotic components for food, shelter and protection. Competition, parasitism and mutualism are interactions among biotic components.

questions.question: The Snapshots list terrestrial ecosystems as forests, grasslands and —
questions.explanation: Snapshots: ecosystems can be terrestrial (forests, grasslands, deserts) or aquatic (ponds, lakes, sea, oceans).

questions.question: In the sequence Individual → Population → Community → Ecosystem, at which level are ABIOTIC components first included?
questions.explanation: Individuals, populations and communities are all made only of living things. Only the ecosystem includes abiotic components such as air, water and soil.

questions.question: Which set names human-made ecosystems created to meet human needs?
questions.explanation: Section 12.9.1 lists fish ponds, farms and parks as artificial ecosystems created by humans.

questions.question: How do human-made ecosystems differ from natural ones?
options: They need human care and management
They have no abiotic components at all
questions.explanation: Well-designed human-made ecosystems can reduce pollution and support biodiversity, but unlike natural ecosystems they need human care and management.

questions.question: Organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis are called —
questions.explanation: Plants make their own food, so they are producers or autotrophs (auto = self, troph = food).

questions.question: The word 'autotroph' comes from roots meaning —
questions.explanation: Auto = self and troph = food: autotrophs feed themselves. Hetero = other (heterotrophs) and sapro = rotten (saprotrophs).

questions.question: Organisms that eat only plants are called —
questions.explanation: Herbivores such as deer and hare eat only plants. Carnivores eat only animals and omnivores eat both.

questions.question: Which animal does the chapter name as an omnivore?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives crows, foxes and mice as omnivores. Deer and hare are herbivores; the leopard is a carnivore.

questions.question: Which pair lists only herbivores named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Deer and hare eat only plants. Crows, foxes and mice are omnivores, and the leopard is a carnivore.

questions.question: A student records a crow as 'feeds on plants: Yes' and 'feeds on animals: Yes' in Table 12.4. The crow should be classified as —
questions.explanation: Organisms that eat both plants and animals are omnivores — the chapter lists crows among them.

questions.question: Which statement about producers and consumers is NOT correct?
options: Mice are herbivores because they eat only plant seeds
Heterotrophs depend on other organisms for their food
A leopard that eats only animals is a carnivore
Green plants that make their own food are autotrophs
questions.explanation: The chapter classifies mice as omnivores (eating both plants and animals), not herbivores.

questions.question: Deer and hare are herbivores because they eat only plants.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives deer and hare as examples of herbivores — organisms that eat only plants.

questions.question: Crows, foxes and mice are carnivores because they eat other animals.
questions.explanation: They eat both plants and animals, so the chapter classifies them as omnivores, not carnivores.

questions.question: Which of these organisms are heterotrophs?
questions.explanation: Deer and vultures cannot make their own food and depend on other organisms. Trees and grass perform photosynthesis, so they are autotrophs.

questions.question: In Table 12.4, which organism would have 'Yes' in the 'Performs photosynthesis' column?
questions.explanation: Only the tree is a green plant that performs photosynthesis. Mushrooms are fungi that grow on dead matter; squirrels and vultures are animals.

questions.question: Why would a mushroom NOT be listed as a producer?
options: It feeds on both plants and animals like an omnivore
It hunts and eats small animals like a carnivore
It does not make its own food but grows on dead matter
It eats only plants and plant products like a herbivore
questions.explanation: Mushrooms are fungi that grow on dead plants or trees, breaking down dead matter — they are decomposers, not producers or consumers in the usual sense.

questions.question: What is a food chain?
options: A simple sequence showing who eats whom in an ecosystem
A network of many interlinked feeding relationships
A list of all the organisms living in one habitat
A pyramid showing the number of each organism
questions.explanation: A food chain is a linear sequence of 'who eats whom'. Interlinked chains form a food web, and a pyramid shows numbers at each level.

questions.question: In the food chain Grass → Hare → Leopard, the arrows point —
options: From the largest organism to the smallest one
From the organism that is eaten to the one that eats it
From the eater to the organism that it eats
From the producer towards the source of sunlight
questions.explanation: Grass is eaten by the hare and the hare by the leopard, so each arrow goes from the food to its consumer.

questions.question: In Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle, at which trophic level is the frog?
questions.explanation: Grass is at the first level, the grasshopper (herbivore) at the second, and the frog (small carnivore) at the third.

questions.question: In Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle, which organism is at the FOURTH trophic level?
questions.explanation: Counting from grass (1), grasshopper (2), frog (3), the snake is at the fourth level and the eagle at the fifth.

questions.question: Large carnivores such as tigers or vultures occupy —
questions.explanation: The chapter places small carnivores like frogs at the third level and large carnivores like tigers or vultures at the next level above them.

questions.question: In Activity 12.7, which organism has the LARGEST number in the crop field and so forms the base of the pyramid?
questions.explanation: The highest count is placed at the base. The millet plants are most numerous, mice fewer, and eagles the fewest at the top.

questions.question: Why is the eagle at the top of the pyramid in Activity 12.7?
options: It has the largest body among the three
It is the only one of the three that can fly
It eats millet as well as mice
It has the lowest number among the three
questions.explanation: The pyramid is built by arranging numbers: the highest number at the base and the lowest at the top. Eagles are fewest, so they sit at the top.

questions.question: A deer eating leaves in a forest occupies which trophic level?
questions.explanation: Herbivores like hares and deer are at the second level, feeding on producers at the first level.

questions.question: In a food chain, herbivores occupy the first trophic level because they are the most numerous consumers.
questions.explanation: Producers (green plants) occupy the first trophic level; herbivores are at the second.

questions.question: Consider Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake. If frogs disappear, what happens to grasshoppers and snakes?
questions.explanation: Frogs eat grasshoppers, so without frogs grasshoppers multiply. Snakes eat frogs, so they lose their food and their numbers fall.

questions.question: Why would grasshopper numbers rise if frogs vanished from the chain Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake?
options: Grass would grow faster without frogs
Their predator in the chain is gone
They would also eat the snakes' food
questions.explanation: In this chain frogs are the only organism that eats grasshoppers, so removing frogs removes the check on the grasshopper population.

questions.question: Which organism is common to both food chains described for the grassland (Grass → Hare → Leopard and Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle)?
questions.explanation: Grass is the producer at the start of both chains; the other organisms appear in only one of them.

questions.question: In the crop-field chain Millet → Mouse → Eagle, the mouse is —
options: A consumer at the second trophic level
A producer at the first trophic level
A consumer at the third trophic level
A decomposer at the top trophic level
questions.explanation: The mouse eats millet (the producer), so here it acts as a consumer at the second level; the eagle eating mice is at the third.

questions.question: Interlinked food chains in an ecosystem form a network called a —
questions.explanation: When food chains are interlinked, the network formed is a food web.

questions.question: Why do food chains in an ecosystem become interlinked?
options: Producers are always found at the top of every food chain
Decomposers connect only the top carnivores in each chain
Each organism may be eaten by two or more types of organisms
Each organism eats exactly one other type of organism only
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that each organism may be eaten by two or more kinds of organisms, so chains cross and link into a web.

questions.question: In the Fig. 12.11 food web (grasses, grasshopper, bird, frog, snake, hawk, fox, hare, mouse, owl), which is the producer?
questions.explanation: Only the grasses make their own food; all the animals listed are consumers.

questions.question: Which organisms in the Fig. 12.11 food web are predators rather than plant-eaters?
questions.explanation: Hawks and snakes eat other animals. The hare is a herbivore and grasses are producers.

questions.question: In Fig. 12.20, grass and plants feed hares and deer, which in turn feed foxes and eagles. If disease cuts the hare population, what is likely?
options: Foxes and eagles get less food, so their numbers may fall
Deer numbers fall because they depend on hares for food
Grass declines since fewer hares spread its seeds
Foxes and eagles increase as they stop competing with hares
questions.explanation: Hares are prey for foxes and eagles; fewer hares means less food for these predators. Deer do not eat hares, and grass would if anything be grazed less.

questions.question: With fewer hares in the Fig. 12.20 web, what might happen to the deer?
options: Deer will increase because they inherit the hares' grass
Predators may hunt deer more, putting pressure on deer numbers
Deer will have fewer plants because hares no longer trim the grass
Deer numbers are unaffected because nothing links them to hares
questions.explanation: Foxes and eagles that lose hares as prey may turn more to deer, the other herbivore in the web — so deer are linked to hares indirectly through shared predators.

questions.question: In a food web, one organism can be connected to several others through feeding relationships.
questions.explanation: A food web shows that each organism may be eaten by, or eat, two or more kinds of organisms.

questions.question: A food web is a single straight line showing who eats whom.
questions.explanation: A single straight line is a food chain. A food web is a network formed when many chains are interlinked.

questions.question: Which statement about food webs is NOT correct?
options: One organism may be eaten by two or more kinds of organisms
Food webs represent feeding relationships in an ecosystem
Removing one organism affects only its direct predator
A food web is formed when food chains are interlinked
questions.explanation: Because organisms are linked in many directions, removing one has cascading effects through the web — as the frog-leg and pond examples show — not just on one predator.

questions.question: Which option correctly compares a food chain and a food web?
options: A chain is linear; a web is a network of interlinked chains
A chain is a network; a web is a single linear sequence
A chain includes decomposers; a web never does
A web has one producer; a chain has many producers
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a food chain as a linear sequence and a food web as the network formed when chains interlink.

questions.question: In Fig. 12.20, which organisms feed DIRECTLY on grass and plants?
questions.explanation: Hares and deer are the herbivores eating grass and plants. Foxes and eagles are predators feeding on the herbivores.

questions.question: Organisms that break down dead plants and animals into simpler substances are called —
questions.explanation: Fungi and bacteria that decompose dead matter are decomposers or saprotrophs (sapro = rotten, troph = food).

questions.question: In the word 'saprotroph', what does 'sapro' mean?
questions.explanation: Sapro = rotten and troph = food — saprotrophs feed on rotten (dead) matter.

questions.question: What does decomposition return to the soil?
questions.explanation: Breaking down dead matter returns important nutrients to the soil, which plants then use — this is why decomposers are called nutrient recyclers.

questions.question: Beetles and flies found on elephant dung help the ecosystem by —
options: Protecting the dung from fungi and bacteria
Breaking it down and recycling nutrients
Spreading seeds contained in the dung
questions.explanation: The chapter says these tiny insects help break down droppings and recycle nutrients back into the environment.

questions.question: If all decomposers suddenly disappeared from a forest, what would happen?
options: Herbivores would increase since more dead plants are available
The soil would become richer as dead matter stays on it
Dead matter would pile up and soil nutrients would not be renewed
Plants would grow faster since nothing would consume them
questions.explanation: Decomposers break dead matter into simpler substances that return nutrients to the soil. Without them, dead matter accumulates and the soil is not replenished.

questions.question: Why is an ecosystem with only producers and no consumers or decomposers not possible?
options: Producers would stop photosynthesis without animals to pollinate them
Producers need consumers to carry their seeds or they cannot reproduce
Producers would run out of sunlight without consumers to share it
Without decomposers, dead matter would never be broken down to recycle nutrients
questions.explanation: Nutrients in soil come largely from decomposition. Without decomposers, dead producers would lock up nutrients and the soil would be depleted; consumers also pass energy and matter along.

questions.question: In nature, nothing is wasted — everything is reused.
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes the decomposition section with exactly this idea: decomposers recycle nutrients so nothing is wasted.

questions.question: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria make their own food like producers do.
questions.explanation: Decomposers feed on dead matter; they are saprotrophs, not autotrophs.

questions.question: Why do migratory birds fly to different habitats in India?
options: To avoid harsh climate and search for food
To pollinate crops growing on Indian farms
To escape predators living in their homeland
To breed only in the wetlands of India
questions.explanation: The chapter says migratory birds come to avoid harsh climate and in search of food.

questions.question: How do migratory birds help farmers?
options: They loosen the soil while searching for worms
They prey on insect pests and control pest populations
They spread fertiliser by dropping dung on the fields
They scare away cattle that trample the crops
questions.explanation: Migratory birds are predators of insect pests, helping farmers control pests and indirectly supporting healthy crop growth.

questions.question: Demoiselle Cranes visit which place during the winter months?
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions Demoiselle Cranes visiting the water body of Khichan village in Jodhpur district in winter.

questions.question: The chapter says migratory birds 'link two habitats'. How?
options: They carry water from one habitat to another in their bodies
They build nests using materials from both of the habitats
They force other birds to move between the two habitats
They act as pollinators or seed dispersers along their migration path
questions.explanation: As they travel, migratory birds pollinate and disperse seeds along their path, connecting the habitats they pass through.

questions.question: Which roles of migratory birds in an ecosystem does the chapter mention?
questions.explanation: Migratory birds keep balance as pollinators or seed dispersers and as predators of pests. They are not decomposers or producers.

questions.question: In Fig. 12.13, what starts the chain of changes in the pond?
options: Plants in the pond die due to pollution
Fish die because of heavy overfishing
Insects increase due to the warm weather
Farmers spray pesticides on their crops
questions.explanation: The chain begins with many pond plants dying because of pollution; everything else follows from this.

questions.question: When fewer plants remain in the pond, what is the immediate effect?
options: More fish survive in the water
Less oxygen is produced in the water
More oxygen is produced in the water
questions.explanation: Plants release oxygen, so with fewer plants less oxygen is produced in the water, leading to a drop in the fish population.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the chain in Fig. 12.13?
options: Plants die → more insects → less oxygen → fish die → crops damaged
Less oxygen → crops damaged → plants die → fish die → more insects
Plants die → less oxygen → fish die → more insects → crops damaged
Fish die → plants die → less oxygen → more insects → crops damaged
questions.explanation: Pollution kills plants, oxygen falls, fish die, fewer consumers means insects increase, and the insects spread to farms where they damage crops.

questions.question: Why do insects increase in number after the fish die in the Fig. 12.13 chain?
options: Dead fish provide extra food for the insects
Pesticides from farms attract insects to the pond
Fewer consumers remain in the pond to eat them
questions.explanation: The chapter says a reduced fish population means fewer consumers in the pond, so insects increase in number.

questions.question: What are farmers compelled to do at the end of the Fig. 12.13 chain?
options: Use pesticides to grow their crops
Dig new ponds for breeding fish
Plant more plants in the pond
Stop growing crops near the pond
questions.explanation: Insects spreading from the pond to farmlands force farmers to use pesticides, which may again harm the environment.

questions.question: The decline in frog populations due to harvesting led to —
questions.explanation: Frogs eat insects, so fewer frogs meant more agricultural pests, which forced farmers to use more synthetic pesticides.

questions.question: How did the Government of India respond to the ecological damage from frog harvesting?
options: It banned the use of synthetic pesticides
It started breeding frogs on farms
It imported frogs from other countries
It banned the export of frog legs
questions.explanation: The Government banned frog-leg exports to prevent further ecological damage.

questions.question: What general lesson does the frog-leg case illustrate?
options: Removing one organism can trigger cascading effects
Pesticides are the main cause of frog decline
Frogs are the only insect-eaters on farms
questions.explanation: Harvesting frogs led to more pests, more pesticides, and harm to soil, water and health — one change led to many others.

questions.question: An ecosystem's balance is dynamic, not fixed, and can be disrupted by natural or human-made changes.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that ecological balance is dynamic and can be disrupted by natural or human-made changes.

questions.question: Ecological balance means populations in an ecosystem stay exactly fixed and never change.
questions.explanation: Balance is dynamic — populations and resources stay stable through interactions, but they are not fixed.

questions.question: Students noticed fewer butterflies in the school garden. Which reason is best supported by the chapter?
options: An increase in mushroom growth in the beds
Pesticide use or fewer flowering plants nearby
Too many earthworms living in the garden soil
More sunlight reaching the garden beds each day
questions.explanation: The chapter links pesticides to harm for natural insect populations and links flowering plants to pollinators; losing either reduces butterflies.

questions.question: Which step would help bring more butterflies back to the campus?
options: Spray synthetic pesticides to kill pests
Replace flowering plants with one lawn grass
Grow more flowering plants and avoid pesticides
Remove all dragonflies from the garden pond
questions.explanation: Flowering plants provide nectar and pollen for butterflies, while pesticides and monoculture harm pollinators.

questions.question: Besides feeding relationships, organisms compete for common resources such as —
options: Food, water, physical space or sunlight
questions.explanation: The chapter lists food, water, physical space and sunlight as the common resources organisms compete for.

questions.question: What role does competition play in an ecosystem?
options: It controls population size and keeps the balance
It lets one species multiply without any limit
It removes all weaker species from the habitat
It increases the total resources in the habitat
questions.explanation: Competition helps control population size; without it one species could multiply too much and cause an imbalance.

questions.question: A relationship in which both organisms benefit is called —
questions.explanation: Mutualism: both benefit, e.g. honeybees and flowers.

questions.question: Orchids growing on trees illustrate which type of relationship?
questions.explanation: The orchid gets physical support while the tree branch is unaffected — one benefits, the other is not affected.

questions.question: Ticks on the body of a dog illustrate which relationship?
questions.explanation: The tick feeds on the dog's blood and benefits, while the dog is harmed (skin irritation) — parasitism.

questions.question: In the orchid-on-tree example, how is the tree branch affected?
questions.explanation: Fig. 12.16 states the tree branch is unaffected while the orchid gets physical support — the defining feature of commensalism.

questions.question: Which statement about relationships between species is NOT correct?
options: In commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected
In parasitism one benefits while the other is harmed
In commensalism the other organism is slightly harmed
questions.explanation: In commensalism the second organism is not affected at all. Harm to one partner is the mark of parasitism.

questions.question: A bird builds its nest on a tree branch and gains shelter, while the tree is neither helped nor harmed. This most resembles a —
questions.explanation: Like the orchid on a tree, one organism benefits and the other is unaffected — commensalism.

questions.question: In the bee–flower relationship, what does the FLOWER gain?
questions.explanation: Fig. 12.16: the bee gets nectar, the flower gets pollinated — both are benefitted.

questions.question: In commensalism, both organisms benefit from the relationship.
questions.explanation: In commensalism one organism benefits while the other is unaffected; both benefitting is mutualism.

questions.question: Without competition, one species could multiply too much and cause an imbalance in the ecosystem.
questions.explanation: The chapter says competition helps control population size and keeps the ecosystem balanced.

questions.question: What did A.J.T. Johnsingh's research prove?
options: Tigers and leopards avoid deer and wild boar
A healthy prey population is key to predator survival
Predators control prey only in small forests
questions.explanation: He showed that predators like tigers and leopards rely on prey such as deer and wild boar, so healthy prey numbers are essential for predators.

questions.question: According to the chapter, which prey animals did Johnsingh find tigers and leopards rely on?
questions.explanation: The box names deer and wild boar as the prey that tigers and leopards rely on.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: Which of these does the chapter list as things forests provide?
questions.explanation: Forests provide fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber and medicines. Water and fish-type food come from aquatic ecosystems.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: The Sundarbans have the world's largest —
questions.explanation: The chapter states the Sundarbans have the largest mangrove forests in the world.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: The Sundarbans are located where which two rivers meet?
questions.explanation: The Sundarbans lie where the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers meet, between India and Bangladesh.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: In which year did UNESCO declare the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site?
questions.explanation: The chapter says UNESCO declared the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site in 1987.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: How do the Sundarbans protect people?
options: By blocking rivers so floods never reach villages
By absorbing all the rain that falls on the coast
By keeping fish away from the coastal farmlands
By slowing strong winds and waves during storms and floods
questions.explanation: The mangroves slow down strong winds and waves during storms and floods, and the trees also absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: Selvam's village in Cuddalore was less affected by the 2004 tsunami than nearby villages. How did mangroves help?
options: They slowed the force of the waves before they reached the village
They absorbed all the sea water so none reached the village
They warned villagers early by swaying strongly in the wind
Their roots raised the land above the level of the tsunami
questions.explanation: Mangrove forests slow down strong winds and waves, so a village behind them receives weaker waves than exposed villages.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: Which threats to the Sundarbans does the chapter mention?
options: Cutting mangroves for fuelwood and farming
Industrial waste and untreated sewage in rivers
questions.explanation: The chapter names cutting mangroves for fuelwood and farming, illegal hunting, overuse of resources, and pollution from industrial waste and untreated sewage.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: The trees of the Sundarbans absorb carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen.
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that Sundarbans trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, one of the ways they protect us.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: The Sundarbans lie between India and Myanmar.
questions.explanation: They lie between India and Bangladesh, where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: Besides food and materials, what other value do ecosystems offer according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Ecosystems also offer aesthetic and recreational value that supports our well-being.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: Which statement about the Sundarbans is NOT correct?
options: Mangrove trees there are cut for fuelwood and farming
It lies where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet
Its World Heritage status has removed all threats
It is home to many endangered plants and animals
questions.explanation: Despite UNESCO status, the chapter says the Sundarbans are 'under a serious threat' from tree cutting, hunting, overuse and pollution.

questions.topic: Benefits of Ecosystems and the Sundarbans
questions.question: According to the chapter, what disturbs the balance in nature?
questions.explanation: The chapter says that when we overuse or misuse natural resources, we disturb the balance in nature.

questions.question: Which problems does the chapter list as damaging ecosystems across India?
questions.explanation: Deforestation, overuse of resources, invasive species, unsustainable land use and pollution are listed. Mangroves and migratory birds help ecosystems.

questions.question: What are protected areas?
options: Land or water set aside to conserve wildlife and their habitats
Farms where crops are grown using only organic manure
Cities where pollution levels are strictly limited by law
Zoos where endangered animals are bred and kept in cages
questions.explanation: Protected areas are parts of land or water set aside to conserve wildlife and their habitats, such as national parks and sanctuaries.

questions.question: Which protected area named in the chapter is in Odisha?
questions.explanation: Chilika Lake is in Odisha. Manas is in Assam, Hemis in Leh and Eaglenest in Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.question: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve is located in the —
questions.explanation: The chapter lists Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (Western Ghats) among India's famous protected areas.

questions.question: Which protected area is correctly matched with its location?
questions.explanation: Hemis is in Leh. Manas is in Assam, Jim Corbett in Uttarakhand, and Eaglenest in Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.question: Which of these are types of protected areas named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter names national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and community conserved areas as protected areas.

questions.question: Protected areas help protect entire habitats, including endangered animals, birds and rare plants.
questions.explanation: The chapter says these places help protect entire habitats including endangered animals, birds and many rare plants.

questions.question: Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary is located in Uttarakhand.
questions.explanation: Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary is in Arunachal Pradesh; Jim Corbett National Park is the one in Uttarakhand.

questions.question: Which statement about threats to ecosystems is NOT correct?
options: Pollution threatens rivers, wetlands and coastal areas
Community conserved areas are a type of protected area
Invasive species help restore damaged grasslands and wetlands
Unsustainable land use damages Indian ecosystems
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the spread of invasive species among the problems damaging ecosystems, not as a remedy.

questions.question: Why do elephants wander into farms and villages?
options: They are attracted by the noise of farm machinery
Farmers plant bananas to lure them away from forests
Corridors direct them straight into villages and farms
Vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry up in their habitat
questions.explanation: When vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry up, elephants search for food like bananas and sugarcane in nearby farms and plantations.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the corridors marked by wildlife ecologists?
options: To connect forest habitats so animals move safely between them
To fence elephants inside a single protected forest area
To guide elephants into farms where they can find food
To separate large predators from their prey animals
questions.explanation: Corridors connect forest habitats, enabling elephants and other wildlife to travel between large forest areas without conflict with human settlements.

questions.question: Which cause-and-effect chain does the chapter give for human–elephant conflict?
options: Habitat loss → more rainfall → forests expand → elephants leave villages
Tree cutting and rainfall change → forests shrink → habitat loss → animals enter villages
Corridors built → forests shrink → elephants lose habitat → crops are damaged
Crop damage → forest clearing → rainfall change → elephants adapt to farms
questions.explanation: Changes in rainfall and temperature plus cutting trees dry and shrink forests; losing habitat pushes animals into human habitats.

questions.question: In which of these states do elephants often enter farms and villages, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter names Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Assam and Chhattisgarh.

questions.question: The Green Revolution increased food production through the use of —
options: Organic manure and natural farming methods
Kunapa Jala and other composted materials
Crop rotation and mixed cropping systems
questions.explanation: In the mid-20th century, tractors, machines, synthetic fertilisers and pesticides raised food production — the Green Revolution.

questions.question: Why are Green Revolution farming methods now considered unsustainable?
questions.explanation: The chapter cites overuse of synthetic chemicals, excessive groundwater extraction and growing only one type of crop. Compost and mixed crops are sustainable practices.

questions.question: How can overuse of synthetic fertilisers reduce soil fertility?
options: By decreasing friendly microorganisms and lowering humus
By increasing earthworms that eat away the humus
By raising soil moisture so nutrients wash away
By attracting pests that consume soil organic matter
questions.explanation: Overuse decreases friendly soil microorganisms and lowers organic matter (humus), which binds soil particles.

questions.question: What role does humus play in soil?
options: It reflects sunlight to cool the soil
It kills pests living in the soil
It supplies oxygen to plant roots
questions.explanation: Humus (organic matter) helps bind soil particles; without enough humus, soil becomes prone to erosion.

questions.question: If humus in a field falls sharply, what does the chapter say is likely?
options: The soil becomes prone to erosion
The soil holds much more water
questions.explanation: Humus binds soil particles, so losing it leaves the soil loose and prone to erosion.

questions.question: How can heavy pesticide use eventually INCREASE pest numbers?
options: It makes crops sweeter, attracting more pests from nearby
It kills the microorganisms that the pests feed on
It warms the soil, which speeds up the breeding of pests
It reduces natural predators that normally keep pests in check
questions.explanation: Fig. 12.18 shows natural control of pests by predators such as beetles; pesticides reduce these predators, so pest populations ultimately increase.

questions.question: What is monoculture?
options: Growing many crops in one field
Growing crops only in one season
questions.explanation: Growing the same crop repeatedly is called monoculture; it can reduce biodiversity and affect pollinators.

questions.question: According to the chapter, monoculture can reduce —
questions.explanation: Monoculture reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators, which are crucial for food production.

questions.question: Heavy irrigation and repeated ploughing can disturb which soil organisms?
questions.explanation: The chapter says these practices disturb soil organisms like earthworms and snails, which help maintain ecological balance.

questions.question: What is Kunapa Jala?
options: A method of ploughing to remove pests from the soil
A liquid fertiliser made by fermenting animal and plant waste
A synthetic pesticide introduced in the Green Revolution
An irrigation technique described in ancient texts
questions.explanation: Kunapa Jala is a liquid fertiliser made from animal and plant waste by fermentation, which breaks complex substances into simpler ones.

questions.question: Synthetic fertilisers and pesticides helped India become food secure.
questions.explanation: The chapter acknowledges that they played a vital role in improving crop production and food security, even though long-term use harms soil.

questions.question: Organic and natural farming methods aim to increase the use of synthetic fertilisers.
questions.explanation: They aim to REDUCE synthetic fertiliser use and support sustainable farming with minimal interference in natural ecosystems.

questions.question: 'Human-made ecosystems like agricultural fields are necessary, but they must be made sustainable.' Which practice supports this?
options: Extracting more groundwater to irrigate heavily
Spraying more pesticide whenever pests resist
Using organic manure and reducing synthetic chemicals
Growing a single commercial crop every season
questions.explanation: Farms feed us but overuse of chemicals, groundwater and monoculture degrade soil; organic manure and fewer chemicals keep farming sustainable.

questions.question: Fig. 12.18 shows a beetle feeding on pests. What does the figure illustrate?
options: Damage to crop leaves by beetles
Natural control of pests by predators
questions.explanation: The caption reads 'Natural control of pests by predators — Beetle feeding on pests', showing why killing predators with pesticides backfires.
